title: ACE: Cloud SQL, Storage Lifecycle, Pub/Sub, Snapshots, and Choosing a Database
intro: The data side of the Associate Cloud Engineer: a managed relational database, storage that gets cheaper as it ages, messaging between services, disk backups, and choosing among Google Cloud's many databases. The project is shop-prod and the region europe-west1.

steps.prompt: Create a highly available PostgreSQL 16 Cloud SQL instance orders-db in europe-west1, with 2 vCPUs and 8 GB of memory, failing over across zones.
expected_commands: gcloud sql instances create orders-db --database-version POSTGRES_16 --region europe-west1 --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --availability-type REGIONAL
steps.fake_output:
Creating Cloud SQL instance for POSTGRES_16...done.
Created [https://sqladmin.googleapis.com/sql/v1beta4/projects/shop-prod/instances/orders-db].
NAME       DATABASE_VERSION  LOCATION        TIER              PRIMARY_ADDRESS  STATUS
orders-db  POSTGRES_16       europe-west1-b  db-custom-2-8192  34.76.12.41      RUNNABLE
steps.explanation: A primary with a standby in another zone of the region.
steps.why: REGIONAL availability is Cloud SQL's high availability: synchronous replication to a standby and automatic failover, like RDS Multi-AZ. Read replicas are separate and serve reads. In production, use private IP and connect through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or connectors, rather than a public address.

steps.prompt: Apply the lifecycle rules in lifecycle.json (Nearline after 30 days, Coldline after 90, delete after 365) to the bucket gs://shop-prod-logs.
expected_commands: gcloud storage buckets update gs://shop-prod-logs --lifecycle-file lifecycle.json
steps.explanation: Objects now move to cheaper classes and expire by themselves.
steps.why: Storage classes differ in minimum storage duration and retrieval cost: Standard (none), Nearline (30 days, about monthly access), Coldline (90, quarterly), Archive (365, yearly). Location type matters too: regional, dual-region, or multi-region, chosen for latency and availability.

steps.prompt: Orders need to notify several downstream services without the checkout service knowing about them. Create a Pub/Sub topic orders.
steps.explanation: Publishers send to the topic; each subscriber gets its own copy through a subscription.
steps.why: Pub/Sub decouples producers from consumers: add a new consumer by adding a subscription, with no change to checkout. It delivers at least once, so consumers must handle duplicates, the same lesson as SQS and Kafka in the Messaging category.

steps.prompt: Create a pull subscription orders-email on the topic orders, with a 60-second acknowledgement deadline.
expected_commands: gcloud pubsub subscriptions create orders-email --topic orders --ack-deadline 60
steps.explanation: The email service pulls order messages and has 60 seconds to acknowledge each.
steps.why: An unacknowledged message is redelivered after the deadline, so the deadline must cover the processing time (the same trap as SQS visibility timeouts). Push subscriptions deliver to an HTTPS endpoint instead, a common pairing with Cloud Run. A dead-letter topic catches messages that keep failing.

steps.prompt: Take a snapshot of the persistent disk worker-1 in zone europe-west1-b before patching, named worker-1-prepatch.
expected_commands: gcloud compute disks snapshot worker-1 --zone europe-west1-b --snapshot-names worker-1-prepatch
steps.explanation: A point-in-time copy of the disk, stored outside the zone.
steps.why: Snapshots are incremental and global, so a disk can be restored in another zone or region. Snapshot schedules (resource policies) make them automatic; a machine image captures the whole VM, configuration and all disks, which is what you want before a risky change to the whole instance.

steps.prompt:
Which database fits a global inventory system that needs relational schemas, strong consistency, and horizontal scale across regions?
  a) Cloud SQL
  b) Spanner
  c) Bigtable
  d) Firestore
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
Cloud SQL : managed MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server, one region, vertical scale
AlloyDB   : PostgreSQL-compatible, faster, still regional
Spanner   : relational, strongly consistent, scales horizontally and globally
Bigtable  : wide-column NoSQL, huge throughput, time series and IoT
Firestore : document database for mobile and web apps
BigQuery  : analytics warehouse, not for transactions
Memorystore: managed Redis/Valkey/Memcached
steps.explanation: Spanner is the only one that is relational, strongly consistent, and global.
steps.why: The ACE asks this mapping in many forms, and the deciding words are usually in the question: 'relational' rules out Bigtable and Firestore, 'global scale' rules out Cloud SQL, 'analytics' points to BigQuery, and 'sub-10 ms reads of time series' points to Bigtable.
